passage:
Monday: Pallavi handed out flyers about the dry lake behind her school. Uday grinned. "Nobody reads those. Does a flyer refill a lake?" Her ears burned, but she only said, "The town office measured the water level last year. I'll bring the numbers."
Thursday: She showed him a printed report and a list of three lakes that were cleaned after local petitions. "It took four years," she admitted. "So yes, it's slow." Uday shrugged. "Slow and pointless are close cousins."
Two Saturdays later: Pallavi was at the lake edge with the cleanup group, pulling plastic from the bank. Uday arrived late, holding a garbage bag. "Just this once," he said. She handed him gloves and didn't gloat.

qa.q: What did Pallavi say she would bring after Uday mocked the flyers?
qa.a: She said she would bring the numbers, since the town office measured the water level last year.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when Uday mocked the flyers, and how does the scene show it?
qa.a: Her ears burned, which suggests hurt or anger, yet she answered with a fact and an offer to bring numbers instead of snapping back.

qa.q: What could Pallavi try if Uday keeps calling her cause pointless?
qa.a: She could keep answering with facts and patience, admit that change is slow, and put her effort into the Saturday cleanups where she can see a real difference.

qa.q: Why might Uday have turned up with a garbage bag after mocking her work?
qa.a: The report may have made him curious, and he seems a little awkward about it, since he arrives late and says "Just this once".

grounding: Shows a teen answering peers' scorn with facts, accepting slow change and acting locally.

passage:
Sunday night: Jahnavi lay on her bed scrolling through the beach villas and rooftop dinners of a travel influencer. Her own room, with its cracked wall and exam timetable, looked very grey.
Wednesday: Rafiq caught her sighing at the phone. "Look at the corner of the reel. It says paid partnership. The villa is free, and the ten bad takes were cut out." 🤔 She looked again and saw the small tag she had never noticed.
Saturday: Instead of comparing, she watched the influencer's tutorial on colour editing. Then she walked to the lane behind her house and filmed steam rising from the tea stall at sunrise. Rafiq texted: "Post it 👍"

qa.q: What small tag did Jahnavi notice on the reel on Wednesday?
qa.a: She noticed the paid partnership tag in the corner of the reel.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling about her own room on Sunday night?
qa.a: Her room looked grey and dull next to the villas and dinners, which suggests envy and a sense that her own life was boring.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi turn her admiration into something useful?
qa.a: She took a skill instead of a lifestyle: she watched the colour editing tutorial and filmed her own lane at sunrise. 😊

qa.q: How might Rafiq have felt watching Jahnavi sigh over the feed?
qa.a: Rafiq probably saw a friend being made to feel small by an edited feed and wanted to gently show what sits behind it.

grounding: Shows a teen envying an influencer, learning the feed is edited and paid, and taking skills rather than comparisons.

passage:
Madhuri read the headline twice: her favourite singer was cancelling his tour because of a family illness. Tears came before she could stop them. She sat on the edge of the bed in the small Pune flat, phone hot in her hand. "He must be so alone," she whispered, and opened his old live video, the one where he says "you guys get me". It calmed her.
Gurpreet knocked, holding two cups of chai. "Crying over him again?"
Madhuri laughed and wiped her face. "I know he doesn't know me. It still feels like he's my friend."
Gurpreet sat down. "Tell me what's actually bugging you. The maths test?"
Madhuri paused, nodded, and put the phone face-down.

qa.q: Why was the singer cancelling his tour?
qa.a: He was cancelling his tour because of a family illness.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri whisper that the singer must be so alone?
qa.a: She feels close to him and imagines his pain as if she knew him, though she also admits he doesn't know her. Her tears show how real the attachment feels.

qa.q: What could Madhuri do to keep enjoying the singer's videos while staying grounded?
qa.a: She can enjoy the comfort of his videos while remembering he doesn't know her, and keep talking to real friends like Gurpreet about what is bothering her. 🤍

qa.q: How might Gurpreet see Madhuri's tears?
qa.a: Gurpreet seems caring rather than mocking, bringing chai and guessing that something else, like the maths test, may be weighing on Madhuri.

grounding: Shows a teen feeling close to a star who does not know her, comforted yet kept connected to a real friend.

passage:
The message arrived after the semi-final, the twelfth from the same fan. "Yamini didi, you're my best friend. I tell you everything. Please say goodnight to me every day. Vaibhav."
Yamini, sixteen and the talk of her Hyderabad badminton club, stood with her racket bag still on her shoulder. Warmth came first, then a small knot. She didn't want to hurt Vaibhav, but she couldn't be someone's daily anchor either. Her coach, passing by, said only, "Take your time with that one."
That night she typed slowly: "Thank you for cheering for me, it really helps. I can't chat every day, but I hope you have friends nearby to share things with. Good luck with school!" She read it twice, sent it, and switched off her phone.

qa.q: How many messages had this fan sent, counting the new one?
qa.a: The new message was the twelfth from the same fan.

qa.q: What was Yamini feeling when she read the message, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt warmth mixed with a small knot of worry: she didn't want to hurt Vaibhav but couldn't be a daily anchor, and she typed slowly and read her reply twice.

qa.q: Why does Yamini's reply work as a kind boundary?
qa.a: It thanks the fan sincerely, says clearly she can't chat every day, and points toward friends nearby, so it appreciates the warmth without feeding dependency.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel opening her reply?
qa.a: Vaibhav may feel a little let down that there will be no daily goodnight, but also glad to be thanked kindly and taken seriously.

grounding: Shows a young public figure receiving a clingy fan letter and answering with warmth and a boundary.

passage:
"It was nothing, the ref is blind!" Marek's voice cracked over the canteen noise in Gdańsk. Santiago slid his phone across the table. The replay showed the striker Marek worshipped stamping on a defender's ankle after the whistle.
"Everyone does that," Marek said, jaw tight, and pushed his tray away. All afternoon he typed angry replies under a critic's post.
That night he watched the replay again, alone and slowly. The stamp was clear. His stomach dropped, not because he liked the player less, but because he had shouted "nothing" so loudly.
Next morning he told Santiago, "Okay. It was a foul. I can still like him and say that."
Santiago nodded. "That's all I wanted."

qa.q: What did the replay show the striker doing?
qa.a: It showed the striker stamping on a defender's ankle after the whistle.

qa.q: Why did Marek's stomach drop when he watched the replay alone?
qa.a: He saw that the foul was real and remembered shouting "nothing" so loudly; he felt uneasy about his fierce defence, not because he liked the player less.

qa.q: What could Marek do next time his idol is criticised?
qa.a: He could listen to the criticism, look at the evidence, and admit what is fair while still liking the player, so loyalty doesn't switch off his own judgment.

qa.q: How might Santiago have seen Marek's outburst in the canteen?
qa.a: Santiago probably saw a friend too heated to look at the replay, and wanted honesty from him rather than for him to stop liking the player.

grounding: Shows a teen defending an idol against fair criticism, then reclaiming his own judgment.

passage:
The group chat lit up every evening at nine, and Aiko loved it. In her bedroom in Osaka she typed jokes about the rival singer's fans, the others sent back laughing faces, and a tight, warm feeling of belonging spread through her chest.
Tonight the target was a girl who had posted a fan drawing. Aiko wrote something cruel about it and got twelve reactions.
Then the girl replied that she was deleting her account, because messages like these had come for three days. Aiko's hands went cold.
Yuki, her classmate, texted her privately: "That was us, wasn't it?"
Aiko stared at the screen for a long time, typed "yes", muted the group and left it. She missed the noise at first, and sat with the quiet.

qa.q: How many reactions did Aiko's cruel message get?
qa.a: It got twelve reactions.

qa.q: Why did Aiko's hands go cold when the girl replied?
qa.a: She realised her joke had hurt a real person who was now deleting her account, and the warm belonging she had enjoyed turned into guilt.

qa.q: What could Aiko do after leaving the group?
qa.a: She could avoid joining such chats again, look for fan spaces that stay kind, and, if she feels able, apologise to the girl or tell an adult if the abuse goes on.

qa.q: How might the girl who posted the drawing have felt over those three days?
qa.a: She probably felt targeted and unwelcome for something she had made with care, which may be why she chose to delete her account.

grounding: Shows a teen joining rival-fan abuse, enjoying belonging, then seeing the hurt and stepping out.

passage:
Dear Rehana,
You know the creator I keep going on about? Yesterday he posted that his "secret trading course" was closing in two hours and only fifty seats remained. Everyone in the comments wrote "joined, life changed". I had Dad's payment app open on the family tablet and my thumb was actually on the button.
Then I remembered what you said about checking who profits. I looked: the same profile was also pushing a betting app, and the comments all sounded alike. I closed the app. That money isn't mine anyway, it's for the rent and Dad's shop.
I told Dad what I nearly did. He wasn't angry, just quiet for a while, and then he thanked me.
Write back soon.
Jyoti

qa.q: What did Jyoti find on the creator's profile besides the course?
qa.a: The same profile was also pushing a betting app.

qa.q: What was Jyoti thinking when she closed the app?
qa.a: She remembered Rehana's advice to check who profits, noticed the alike comments and the tight deadline, and realised the money wasn't hers to spend.

qa.q: What could Jyoti do if the creator posts another countdown offer?
qa.a: She can treat the countdown as pressure, check the claims, ask a trusted adult before anything involving money, and never spend what isn't hers.

qa.q: How might Jyoti's dad have felt on hearing what she nearly did?
qa.a: His quiet suggests worry, and his thanks suggest he was relieved and grateful that she told him.

grounding: Shows a teen recognising a creator monetising fans' trust and stopping before spending money that is not hers.

passage:
Five a.m. That's the part nobody puts on posters. I'm Aditi, and Ishita, you asked why I stopped pinning the runner's photos and started pinning her schedule. I read that she trained through school exams and two failed trials before her first medal.
So I copied a habit, not the image. Three mornings a week I run before school, slowly, and I tick each day in a notebook. Some days I honestly hate it. Last week I skipped once and felt guilty, and then I went out the next morning anyway.
My cousin says I'm copying her. But I'm not trying to become her. I'm trying to become someone who turns up for my own goals. That's what her story gave me: fuel.

qa.q: How many mornings a week does Aditi run before school?
qa.a: She runs three mornings a week before school.

qa.q: What does Aditi mean when she says she isn't trying to become the runner?
qa.a: She wants the runner's habit of turning up for her own goals, not her image, so her admiration works as fuel for her own effort.

qa.q: What would you advise Aditi on a day she hates the run?
qa.a: Keep the routine small, tick the notebook, and remember that the runner's success came from years of discipline, including failed trials. 👍

qa.q: Why might Aditi's cousin see her running differently?
qa.a: The cousin may think Aditi is only imitating the athlete, without seeing that she wants the discipline rather than the fame.

grounding: Shows a teen admiring an athlete's years of discipline and copying habits rather than image.

passage:
Civics teacher's note, Class 10, Friday.
After the assembly where a visiting youth leader spoke, Jaya came to my desk glowing and repeated whole lines of his speech. Her friend Gautam rolled his eyes and said it was only words. I did not correct either of them.
I asked Jaya, "What did he say he has actually done?" She was quiet, then said she didn't know. We looked up the group's public reports together. She wrote three questions in her notebook: what they have built, who pays for it, and what is not in the speech.
She told me the speech still gave her goosebumps, and I said she is allowed that. I will check in on Monday.

qa.q: What three questions did Jaya write in her notebook?
qa.a: She wrote what they have built, who pays for it, and what is not in the speech.

qa.q: What was Jaya feeling after the speech, and how do you know?
qa.a: She felt thrilled: she came to the desk glowing, repeated whole lines, and later said the speech still gave her goosebumps.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped Jaya think for herself?
qa.a: The teacher asked what the leader had actually done and looked up the public reports with her, without lecturing, so Jaya wrote her own questions.

qa.q: Why might Gautam have rolled his eyes?
qa.a: Gautam may be wary of big speeches and think they are only words, though the eye roll alone doesn't show what he really thinks.

grounding: Shows a teen thrilled by a leader's speech and guided to ask what he does, who benefits and what is hidden.

passage:
On Saturday night Kwame lay on his bed in Accra with the phone above his face, scrolling: Rania's cousins at the coast, the class in matching outfits at a birthday, a friend on a mountain holiday. Each picture tightened his chest a little. He had stayed home to help his uncle with the shop stock.
He stopped, thumb hovering. He remembered posting just one photo from last month's football final, and not the argument with the coach afterwards. Highlights, he thought.
He set a timer on the phone, then typed to Rania: "Your coast pics look amazing 🙂 Want to watch the match with me on Sunday?"
Rania replied within a minute: "Yes! I've missed hanging out ❤️"

qa.q: Why had Kwame stayed home that weekend?
qa.a: He had stayed home to help his uncle with the shop stock.

qa.q: What was Kwame thinking when he remembered his own football photo?
qa.a: He realised people post only highlights, as he had, and leave out things like the argument with the coach, so feeds don't show whole lives.

qa.q: What small steps helped Kwame move past the envy?
qa.a: He set a timer to limit his scrolling and messaged Rania to invite a real hangout instead of comparing.

qa.q: How might Rania have felt receiving Kwame's message?
qa.a: Rania seems happy and a little relieved, replying within a minute that they had missed hanging out. 😊

grounding: Shows a teen feeling left out by friends' posted highlights and choosing a timer and a message instead.
